title: Magnesium availability reveals decoupling between growth, photosynthesis and calcification in Gephyrocapsa huxleyi
content:
Abstract

Gephyrocapsa huxleyi is a ubiquitous producer of particulate inorganic carbon (PIC) in the modern ocean, yet the cellular control of calcification remains poorly understood. We combined physiological measurements with proteome profiling to test how external magnesium affects growth, photosynthesis, and calcification across a 0–210 mM Mg gradient. Mg availability affected cell division and cell size differently. Growth rate slowed under Mg limitation, and cell size decreased linearly as Mg increased. Photosynthetic performance was largely maintained from 5.46 to 210 mM Mg. Chlorophyll a content primarily scaled with cell size rather than Mg concentration, and photosynthesis-related proteins shifted only modestly. Pronounced disruption occurred only at 0 mM Mg, where proteomic changes matched the physiological response to complete Mg depletion. In contrast, calcification was highly Mg sensitive. Cellular CaCO3 content decreased linearly from 10.5 to 210 mM Mg, and this trend persisted after accounting for cell size. Coccolith geometry remained largely preserved despite reduced mineralization, and detected candidate calcification-associated proteins did not covary with CaCO3 content, consistent with a strong physicochemical constraint on mineral deposition and limited compensation at the level of detected protein abundance. Together, these results show that photosynthesis is buffered across Mg variation, whereas calcite deposition remains externally constrained, linking Mg availability to division timing and to limits on intracellular mineralization, with implications for the mechanism and rate of PIC production.
